Threat.value: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Callum is a 38-year-old high school history teacher of Scottish descent, married and living in a mid-sized American city. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after being mugged at knifepoint in a parking garage adjacent to a shopping centre on a Saturday afternoon. He had been returning to his car with his arms full of bags when two men closed in on him rapidly from either side, one pressing a blade against his ribs while the other rifled through his pockets and tore his watch from his wrist. The garage was crowded with weekend shoppers, and Callum remembers the specific smell of exhaust and damp concrete, the metallic taste of adrenaline flooding his mouth, and the sound of a car horn somewhere behind him that he initially mistook for a shout. No one intervened. He was left standing between two parked cars, shaking, as the men disappeared into the crowd. The police took a report, offered little, and the case was never pursued. Callum drove himself home that day, his wife in the passenger seat, neither of them knowing yet how completely that afternoon would reorganise his life.

In the weeks that followed, Callum found himself unable to stop the memory from returning without invitation. It would arrive without warning during lessons - the taste of that metallic flood suddenly present on his tongue, the full sensory weight of the moment reconstituting itself so completely that he would lose the thread of what he had been saying and have to grip the edge of his desk until the classroom reasserted itself around him. The intrusive quality of these recollections was not like ordinary remembering; they carried him back bodily, every sense engaged at once, the knife at his ribs as present as the whiteboard in front of him. When the memory surfaced, it reliably deepened his conviction that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place - a belief that had calcified quietly over months into something that now felt like simple fact rather than fear. And the memory, in returning, seemed to prime the very conditions that would summon it again: crowded spaces, the sensation of being hemmed in, the sound of a sudden loud noise in the corridor between classes - each of these could collapse the distance between then and now.

His classroom, once a comfortable domain, became a source of daily vigilance. Callum began arriving early to note where the exits were, positioning himself so that no student could approach from behind him unexpectedly. When a chair scraped suddenly across the floor or a door slammed, he would flinch and scan the room with an urgency he recognised as disproportionate but could not suppress. He had come to study the faces and body language of everyone who entered - students, colleagues, parents at open evenings - reading for signs of threat the way he once read historical documents for subtext. This hypervigilant scanning, far from reassuring him, kept returning him to the memory: the faces of the two men, the speed with which ordinary strangers had become dangerous, the crowd that had simply flowed around him as though nothing were happening. Each time he caught himself cataloguing exits or reading a stranger's posture for menace, it reinforced his certainty that the world warranted exactly this level of watchfulness, and that to relax it would be naive.

The sense of injustice ran deep and had not softened with time. Nothing had been done. The institution - the police, the system - had absorbed his report and returned nothing. Callum had come to believe that this outcome was not incidental but representative: that the world is dangerous and those charged with managing that danger are indifferent. These appraisals, when they surfaced, had a way of pulling the memory forward again, as though his mind were repeatedly returning to the evidence on which the verdict was based. Driving with his wife, who sometimes sat in the passenger seat exactly as she had on the day he drove home from the garage, had become nearly unbearable; the configuration alone was enough to trigger the full sensory return.

What finally brought Callum to seek help was a parent-teacher conference at which he had been so distracted by monitoring the room for threat that he could not recall a single conversation afterward. His wife had noticed the change in him long before he acknowledged it himself. He came to the intake session hoping, he said quietly, to be able to sit in a room without planning how to leave it.
